title: Where Are the Women? Female Finishers Across Southeast Asia's Races
seo_title: Women Runners in Southeast Asia: Female Finishers by Race
meta_description: Women are 35% of finishers across 75 Southeast Asian races: nearly half of 10K fields, a quarter of halves and under a fifth of marathons. The share by country and race, and women-only races.
dek: Women make up about a third of the finishers in Southeast Asia's road races, but the share falls steeply as the distance grows. Here is what 238,642 results show by distance, country and race, how women's times compare, and where women-only races fit.

sections.heading: One in three finishers, and fewer the longer the race
paragraphs: Run SEA holds official results for 75 races in six countries, run between October 2025 and November 2026: 238,642 finishers, almost all with a recorded sex. Women are 82,989 of them, or 34.9% [1].

The share depends heavily on distance. In the 10K, women are close to half the field: the median race is 48% female, and women outnumbered men in 26 of the 68 10K races. In the half marathon, the median race is 26% female. In the marathon it is 18%, about one finisher in five or six [1].

The marathon figure barely moves from race to race. Among the 20 marathons with at least 100 finishers, the female share runs from 9.9% at the BTN UI Green Marathon in Depok, Indonesia (121 finishers) to 25.9% at the Isla del Fuego Marathon on Siquijor in the Philippines (201). The Singapore Marathon, the region's biggest field in our data with 9,294 marathon finishers, is 18.6% female [1].

sections.heading: By country: the Philippines leads, Vietnam trails
paragraphs: In the marathon, every country with more than one race sits between 17% and 19% female. The Malaysia Marathon, the one Malaysian marathon in the data, is lower at 13.8% [1].

The differences open up at shorter distances. Pooling every finisher in each country, the half marathon is 32.6% female in the Philippines (45 races) and 32.2% in Singapore, against 28.0% in Thailand, 26.7% in Indonesia, 25.5% in Malaysia and 24.7% in Vietnam [1].
The 10K shows the same order. Philippine 10Ks are 52.2% female, and women outnumbered men in 24 of the 44. Thailand's are 43.2% female, Vietnam's 42.0%, Singapore's 40.7% and Indonesia's 40.4% [1].

sections.heading: The races with the most and fewest women
paragraphs: The most female field in the data is the Sunnies Run in Makati, a RUNRIO race named after a Philippine eyewear brand. Its 10K was 66.4% female across 4,807 finishers, and its half marathon 47.3% female across 2,811, the highest half-marathon share of any race. Women also outnumbered men in the 10Ks of the HOKA Midnight Run's Cagayan de Oro (60.9%) and Cebu (59.3%) legs and at Isla del Fuego (59.1%) [1].
In absolute numbers, the Singapore Marathon weekend had the most women: 11,445 female finishers across its 10K, half and marathon. The Manila Marathon had 7,585 and Maybank Marathon Bali 3,803 [1].

The lowest shares come from two kinds of race. Some are fast, competitive fields: the National MILO Marathon's Subic leg had the least female half marathon (11.0% of 172), and MILO's 21K closed at 2 hours 30 at its 2026 Cebu and Passi legs [2], a limit that 62% of all half-marathon finishers in our data would miss [1]. Others are regional races with small female fields, such as Blue Ocean Minang Run in Padang (11.5% of its 624 half-marathon finishers) and Buasawan Marathon in Thailand (29.3% of its 10K, the lowest 10K share) [1].

sections.heading: How women's times compare
paragraphs: The median female marathon finisher in our data runs 5:43, and the median man 5:21, a gap of 7%. In the half marathon the medians are 2:55 and 2:36, a 13% gap, and in the 10K 1:30 and 1:18, a 16% gap [1].

The gap narrowing as the distance grows is probably about who enters rather than about speed. With women only 18% of marathon fields, the women who do enter a marathon here are a more selected group than the women in a 10K.

Race by race, the marathon gap varies from 2.6% at the Singlife Davao Marathon to 14.1% at Khun Dan Marathon in Thailand. Fast times are still mostly male: women were 11% of the marathon finishers under four hours and 11% of the half-marathon finishers under two [1].

sections.heading: Women-only races: real, but small in number
paragraphs: Women-only and women-focused races exist in the region, but they are a handful of events, not a trend in the data. Singapore's Great Eastern Women's Run is the best known. Its 19th edition in 2025 drew more than 12,000 women, with a 21.1 km elite race, 10 km and 5 km races and family runs [3]. That is a large race, but not one of the region's largest events: the Singapore Marathon weekend alone had 34,255 finishers in our data, and 11,445 of them were women [1]. Its 2026 edition, set for 1 November at the National Stadium, was cancelled by the organiser [2].

In the Philippines, All Women's Run Asia held its third edition on 30 March 2025 at SM Mall of Asia, with distances from 500 m to 21 km, run to raise awareness of violence against women [4]. Women's Run PH has its first half marathon on 13 March 2027 at the same venue, for International Women's Month. Its categories include a 10 km women's race and a 10 km buddy race [5], so it is women-focused rather than strictly women-only. In Indonesia, AIMS lists the Indonesia Women Half Marathon with a last edition on 11 May 2025 and a next one on 20 June 2027 [6].

Safety is part of the case for these events. A 2023 adidas survey of 9,000 runners aged 16 to 34 in nine countries, none of them in Southeast Asia, found that 92% of women were concerned for their safety while running, and 51% feared being physically attacked, against 28% of men [7].

sections.heading: What the numbers suggest
paragraphs: Women already make up nearly half of Southeast Asia's 10K fields and more than a quarter of its half-marathon fields. The drop comes at the marathon, where the share is stuck below a fifth almost everywhere.

For a woman choosing a first race, the data points to the Philippines' big city 10Ks and halves, where fields are closest to even, and to large fields such as Singapore and Manila, where thousands of other women run every distance. Finish-time figures for the races in our data are in the Lab at runsea.run/tools/.

faqs.question: What share of race finishers in Southeast Asia are women?
faqs.answer: About 35% across 238,642 finishers of 75 races in Run SEA's results data. The share falls with distance: the median 10K is 48% female, the median half marathon 26% and the median marathon 18%. The Philippines has some of the most female half-marathon and 10K fields.

faqs.question: Are women-only races common in Southeast Asia?
faqs.answer: No. There are a handful, such as Singapore's Great Eastern Women's Run (over 12,000 women in 2025; its 2026 edition was cancelled), All Women's Run Asia in Manila and the Indonesia Women Half Marathon. Most women race in mixed fields, where they are nearly half of 10K finishers.

faqs.question: How much slower are women's marathon times in Southeast Asia?
faqs.answer: The median female marathon finisher runs 5:43 against 5:21 for men, a 7% gap. The gap is wider over shorter distances, 13% in the half and 16% in the 10K, probably because the relatively few women who enter marathons are a more selected group than the women in shorter races.

editorial_notes: Rewritten 6 Nov 2026 around data/finish-times (75 races, 238,642 finishers; 703 with no recorded sex excluded from shares). Medians of race-level shares are across all races at that distance; extremes quoted only for fields of 100+. Fixes the old piece: GEWR is no longer called one of the region's largest events, the unsourced 'daylight' and 'growing trend' claims are gone, and the 2026 cancellation is noted from the race record with no cause stated. All external sources opened 6 Nov 2026; the adidas survey is global (no SEA countries) and labelled as such.
